name: Error management theory
statement: Error management theory holds that selection biased judgement under uncertainty towards the cheaper mistake, so some errors are design features rather than flaws.
meaning: This is a framework, not a finding. It says that when a judgement can go wrong in two directions and one direction cost more over evolutionary time, the deciding mechanism should lean towards the cheaper error. A smoke alarm is the standard illustration: missed fires cost more than false alarms, so the alarm is set to cry wolf. Haselton and Buss applied the logic to reading the opposite sex and derived two predictions. Men should overperceive women's sexual interest, because a missed opportunity cost an ancestral man more than a wasted approach. Women should underperceive men's intent to commit, because trusting a man who leaves cost an ancestral woman more than waiting too long. The same logic has been attached to hearing approaching sounds, judging heights and detecting agents. Haselton and Nettle restated it in 2006 under the broader label adaptive bias, and that paper is the one usually cited for the general claim. Because the content of any prediction lives in an assumed cost matrix, the framework's record has to be read prediction by prediction. Nothing follows from the theory until somebody states which error was dearer, and that premise is rarely measured.

origin.who: Martie G. Haselton and David M. Buss
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: The paper names the theory and reports two questionnaire studies of American undergraduates, 217 in Study 1 and 289 in Study 2. Men's overperception of women's sexual intent was already an established finding it set out to explain, credited in the text to Abbey's work from 1982 onwards. The new prediction was women's commitment scepticism.

evidence:
Study 1 asked 113 men and 104 women to rate three statements about commitment and eight behaviours for sexual interest. Women rated men's commitment avoidance higher, 4.52 against men's own 3.96 on a seven-point scale, F(1, 213) = 10.63, p < .01. Ratings of women's commitment did not differ by sex of rater. The sexual-intent items produced no interaction at all, only a main effect of rater: men gave higher ratings than women, 3.70 against 3.39, F(1, 211) = 6.73, p = .01. The authors say this may mean women underperceive men's sexual intent, or that men's overperception extends to targets of both sexes.

Study 2 came in two parts, and the paper keeps their numbers apart. Part 1 rated 15 dating cues against a self-report criterion. Women judged men's commitment intent lower than men judged their own, 1.21 against 1.65, F(1, 279) = 31.58, p < .001. Men judged women's sexual intent higher than women judged themselves, 1.02 against 0.13, F(1, 270) = 28.84, p < .001. Women also rated men's sexual intent above men's self-ratings, 1.42 against 1.10, F(1, 273) = 2.40, p = .02, printed in that form in the paper, which says the result contradicts a general oversexualisation account. Part 2 used a different instrument on a seven-point scale from -3 to +3, with two criterion measures, same-sex ratings and self-ratings. Both predicted biases cleared both criteria there. Men rated women's sexual intent at 0.12 against women's rating of women at -0.34, F(1, 283) = 11.70, p < .01, and against women's self-rating of -1.69, F(1, 283) = 136.89, p < .001. Women rated men's commitment at -1.27 against men's rating of men at -0.99, F(1, 281) = 4.80, p < .02, and against men's self-rating of 0.55, F(1, 281) = 156.25, p < .001.

The sibling test used 131 eligible participants and a subset of the Part 2 items. Men rated their sisters' sexual intent at -1.03 against 0.02 for other women, F(1, 57) = 23.62, p < .001. Women, for whom no prediction had been made, rated their brothers at -0.50 against 1.37 for other men, F(1, 70) = 111.94, p < .001.

Haselton's 2003 survey moved the question to remembered events, asking people how often the opposite sex had misread them. Its design is described here from Bendixen's account rather than from the paper itself, which was not opened. Henningsen and Henningsen put 111 man-woman dyads into face-to-face conversation with strangers. Their abstract reports support for the theory with potential boundary conditions, and separately reports evidence that people project their own level of interest in sex or in commitment onto a partner.

Haselton and Nettle's 2006 review is where the programme states its full scope. It derives the model mathematically and tabulates twelve domains in which it says a cost asymmetry has produced a bias. Table 1 covers five protective cases: approaching sounds, dangerous animals, dangerous persons, food aversions and diseased persons. Table 2 covers seven social ones: inferring human agency, sinister attribution, dispositional inference, cooperation with others, men's perception of women's sexual interest, women's perception of men's commitment, and beliefs in personal control and efficacy. The paper is candid about which came first. It writes that some of the effects it reviews were predicted in advance using error management logic, and names four: women's commitment underperception, the overinclusiveness of disease avoidance, the social exchange heuristic and the negative forgiveness bias. It does not say the list is complete, and it does not say when each of the other cases was found. It then offers new predictions of its own, including an interloper effect of overinferring other people's sexual interest in one's own partner, a bias in men towards overinferring extra-pair interest when a partner is near midcycle, and enhanced disease-avoidance biases in pregnant women.

Outside mating, the auditory looming bias is the most cited case. Neuhoff's 1998 abstract reports that listeners overestimated the change in level of rising tones relative to equivalent falling tones, and that the bias was stronger at higher levels. Neuhoff, Planisek and Seifritz report in four experiments that both sexes underestimate the time to arrival of approaching sounds, that the bias is stronger in women, and that no sex difference appears for the perceived distance of receding sounds. Merz and colleagues, summarising the earlier work, state that looming sounds are heard as changing more sharply than matched receding sounds and are expected to arrive sooner than they do. Baumgartner and colleagues reproduced a looming asymmetry using spectral cues at constant intensity, which answers the objection that the effect was about loudness rather than distance.

replication.headline: The survey pattern behind the sexual overperception bias replicates in Norway and Japan and a weapon-possession prediction replicates directly, while larger tests on looming sounds, snake search, disease avoidance and hormones found no bias.
replication.detail:
Bendixen ran a direct replication of Haselton's 2003 survey on Norwegian students, chosen because Norway is more gender-egalitarian than the United States. Of 400 questionnaires, 344 came back, eight extreme cases were removed, and 308 remained, 181 women and 127 men. Over their lifetimes 88.3% of women reported having been sexually overperceived against 39.4% underperceived, while for men the two figures were 70.6% and 74.6%. For the past year, women reported overperception far more often than underperception, t(180) = 10.76, p < .001, d = 0.94, and the same contrast in men was much smaller, t(126) = 3.76, p < .001, d = 0.29. Bendixen estimates the corresponding figures in Haselton's original at d = 0.80 for women and d = 0.16 for men, using Cortina and Nouri's formula applied to the original's reported statistics. Those two numbers are Bendixen's calculation, not Haselton's, and are quoted here as such. Hiraishi, Murasaki, Okuda and Yamate ran a preregistered replication in Japan on 330 people, 165 of each sex, recruited through a commercial web panel rather than a university. All were single, aged 18 to 24 and without children, and about half were students. The predicted interaction held, and the simple effect of type of misperception was significant only for women, F(1, 328) = 12.987 for lifetime experience and F(1, 328) = 16.015 for last year's frequency, both p < .001.

What those surveys measure is how often people say they were misread. Studies that compare a perceiver's judgement with a target's own report have gone the other way. Lee, Sidari, Murphy, Sherlock and Zietsch ran 1,226 speed daters, 586 men and 640 women. Men overperceived and women underperceived, and the sex difference became negligible once the raters' sociosexual orientation and their tendency to project their own interest onto partners were entered as mediators. The authors state this challenges the idea that the sex difference is a specialised adaptation. Henningsen and Henningsen had already found the projection effect in 111 dyads in 2010.

The theory's own novel prediction has been tested less often. Brown and Olkhov report that women did not show the commitment-scepticism bias when given behavioural evidence that a partner was willing to commit, which they read as functional flexibility rather than a standing bias, and that women needed more such evidence than men before feeling certain of a partner's commitment.

Perilloux and Kurzban attacked the inference rather than the data. Across three studies they reproduced the sex difference, showed men held to their ratings when paid for accuracy, and showed women think other women understate their intentions. Their conclusion is that men may be reading women correctly and managing error through biased behaviour instead of biased belief. Murray, Murphy, von Hippel, Trivers and Haselton replied with a preregistered test of the competing predictions and concluded that men do overestimate. Perilloux and Kurzban published a reply in the same issue. None of the three papers could be read beyond its title and record, and their contents are described here from the 2015 abstract and from the titles of the 2017 exchange.

Brandner, Pohlman and Brase re-analysed the measurement itself with signal detection theory. In their Study 1, on relatively clear signals, sensitivity to interest and disinterest drove what people reported rather than a standing bias towards seeing interest, and cues of interest were underperceived overall. The apparent male bias came from error management's use of difference scores, which hide where each sex starts. Their Study 2, on more ambivalent scenarios, largely reproduced that pattern, except that the error management analysis there made men's misperception significantly larger than women's.

The auditory prediction has now failed a direct test. Merz and colleagues used a probe comparison task from the representational momentum literature to ask where a changing sound is heard to end. The adaptive account predicts a forward shift for approaching sounds. Every changing-intensity condition in both experiments gave a negative, backward shift, and there was no effect of intensity change direction in Experiment 1, F(1, 29) = 0.91, p = .347. Complex tones in Experiment 2 shifted further backwards than pure tones, F(1, 60) = 4.51, p = .038, again against prediction. Experiment 2 also carried a no-change baseline, and once scores were corrected against it the decreasing stimuli still shifted backwards at -0.41 while the increasing stimuli were judged accurately at 0.01. That is a difference between approaching and receding sounds without the forward shift the adaptive account requires.

Three of the protective domains have since been tested directly. Tybur, Jones, DeBruine, Ackerman and Fasolt preregistered a replication of Miller and Maner's finding that recently ill people attend more to disfigured faces. The original tested 96 people and reported that the 28 recently ill took 38 ms longer to identify targets after disfigured-face distractors than after typical ones, dz = 0.58. The replication analysed 402 people at three universities after eleven preregistered exclusions. The interaction between illness recency and face type came to F(1, 400) = 1.87, partial eta squared = .005, 90% CI [.000, .027], p = .173, and an equivalence test ruled out an effect as large as dz = 0.35. Attention to disfigured faces appeared in both groups, not only in the recently ill.

Zsido and colleagues bear on the snake case, which the 2006 review calls one of its best researched examples. Their paper is framed against the attentional prioritisation literature and does not mention error management theory. Two preregistered experiments varied how often a target appeared among 32 objects scattered on the screen, at 10% or 50% prevalence. They analysed 115 people from 119 recruited at Pécs and 109 from 113 at New Mexico State, 224 in total. Search for snake targets was slower and less accurate than search for rabbits, the reverse of the predicted prioritisation.

The pregnancy prediction is unsettled. The compensatory prophylaxis hypothesis holds that disgust rises when immune function is suppressed, and Haselton and Nettle drew the pregnant case from Fessler's version of that argument. Jones and colleagues tested 375 women weekly in blocks of five sessions, 337 of whom completed five sessions or more, and tracked salivary progesterone against the pathogen subscale of the Three Domain Disgust Scale. Nothing moved. Progesterone gave an estimate of 0.32, t = 0.74, p = .46, oestradiol 0.30, t = 0.61, p = .55, testosterone 0.35, t = 0.71, p = .48, and cortisol 0.02, t = 0.06, p = .95.

Dlouhá, Roberts, Hlaváčová, Nouzová and Kaňková recruited 106 Czech women and analysed 94, measured in each trimester and six to fourteen weeks after birth. They set out to replicate Żelaźniewicz and Pawłowski, who had found core disgust highest in the first trimester. Disgust moved the other way. Overall scores changed across the four measurements, F(3, 234.4) = 3.06, p = 0.029, as did animal-reminder disgust, F(3, 234.4) = 5.97, p < 0.001, both rising from the first trimester; core disgust did not change, F(3, 235.1) = 0.36, p = 0.783. Women reporting recent illness in the first trimester scored higher at that point on core disgust, F(1, 83) = 6.40, p = 0.013, and on contamination disgust, F(1, 83) = 5.64, p = 0.020, though the paper states it will not discuss the contamination subscale because its internal reliability was low. The authors split their own verdict. The rising pattern is not consistent with the hypothesis as Fessler and Żelaźniewicz conceived it, they write, while the same rise tracks the rise in progesterone through pregnancy, which they say could support it.

One prediction has replicated directly. Moser, Ellk, Jones and Holbrook preregistered a direct replication of Holbrook and colleagues' finding that a person holding an everyday object with lethal affordances is read as angrier. They collected 626 and analysed 476, against 264 in the original. Targets holding a kitchen knife were rated higher in state anger, t(457) = 3.64, p < .001, d = 0.34, in trait anger, t(460) = 2.19, p = .029, d = 0.20, and in trait unpleasantness, t(453) = 4.44, p < .001, d = 0.41. Trait fear, disgust and dishonesty showed no effect of the object, and the exploratory prediction that a friend of the armed man would also be read as angrier failed.

Sex-specificity fares worst of all. In a preregistered study of 710 adults from Buss's own laboratory, Baca, Costello, Hahnel-Peeters, Thomas, Schmitt and Buss found that men overestimated women's desire for sexual variety, and that women showed the same bias about men, and that both sexes overestimated their own sex too.

study.cite: Bendixen, M. (2014). Evidence of systematic bias in sexual over- and underperception of naturally occurring events: A direct replication of Haselton (2003) in a more gender-equal culture. Evolutionary Psychology, 12(5), 1004-1021.

limits:
The structured effect size is one contrast from one replication: women's reported frequency of being overperceived against being underperceived over the past year. It is not a measure of anyone's perceptual accuracy, and it does not summarise the theory. No effect size is given for the original studies, because Haselton and Buss report F tests and condition means and no standardised effect, and because the 2003 survey could not be read. Bendixen's estimates of the original's effect sizes are his arithmetic on the original's statistics and are reported on this page as his.

Several papers were located but not read in full, and the reasons differ. On 21 September 2026, Haselton's 2003 article, Neuhoff's 2001 paper, the 2017 exchange between Murray and colleagues and Perilloux and Kurzban, and La France, Henningsen, Oates and Shaw's 2009 meta-analyses were all recorded as closed by Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar, with no abstract deposited at Crossref, Europe PMC or PubMed and no copy on the authors' university pages. The publisher pages for Neuhoff 2001 and the 2017 exchange returned a bot challenge rather than a paywall notice, so a reader arriving by another route may get further. Neuhoff's 1998 abstract is readable at the Nature page and is quoted above; its full text is not. What the 2001 experiments found is stated here on Merz and colleagues' summary of them. No effect size from the 2009 meta-analyses appears here, and Haselton and Galperin cite them only as a recent meta-analysis, without figures.

Two further cases are open access that this session could not read in full. McKay and Efferson's accepted manuscript is deposited at the University of Zurich repository and Brandner, Pohlman and Brase's article is free at Elsevier, and on 21 September 2026 both hosts answered requests for the file with automated bot challenges, Anubis and Cloudflare respectively. Both abstracts were reached by another route, at Semantic Scholar for Brandner and through the Zurich repository's OAI-PMH record for McKay, and the arguments on this page are described from those. The published version of Jones and colleagues is behind the same Cloudflare challenge at ScienceDirect; the accepted manuscript was read instead.

No multi-site replication, registered replication report or meta-analysis of error management theory as such was found. On 21 September 2026 the search covered Crossref, Europe PMC, PubMed, Semantic Scholar and Unpaywall, including Europe PMC queries pairing the theory's name with meta-analysis, registered replication, many labs and multi-site. Preregistration exists at the level of individual studies: Murray and colleagues in 2017, Zsido and colleagues in 2024, Moser and colleagues in 2025, Baca and colleagues in 2026, Hiraishi and colleagues in 2016 and Tybur and colleagues in 2020.

Obrecht and Agrillo reviewed the sexual overperception literature under PRISMA in 2026 and put the mean participant age across studies at 22.9 years, with participant age rising over time, F(1, 81) = 13.49, p < 0.001, r = 0.38. They state that they are aware of no attempt to replicate the findings in samples aged 40 or over.

The deeper limit is that the framework's record is an inventory rather than a verdict. Haselton and Nettle tabulate twelve domains. This entry located direct tests in six of them: approaching sounds, dangerous animals, dangerous persons, diseased persons, men's perception of women's sexual interest and women's perception of men's commitment. The other six were not examined here. Two of them, beliefs in personal control and the inference of human agency, have their own entries in this atlas under illusion of control and agent detection, and neither is written as a test of error management. For food aversions, sinister attribution, dispositional inference and cooperation with others, this entry makes no claim either way. The dangerous-persons test on this page, Moser and colleagues on weapon possession, is the one that came out for the theory.

Of the new predictions the 2006 paper offers, no test of the interloper effect or of the fertility-linked infidelity bias was found. On 21 September 2026, Europe PMC returned no hits for 'interloper bias', none for 'interloper effect' paired with mate, none for Smurda as an author, and none for ovulation or midcycle paired with infidelity and overinference, and a Crossref bibliographic search on the same terms returned nothing on the topic. Searches by the original authors' names returned later ovulatory-cycle work by Haselton and colleagues, none of it a test of either prediction. The 2006 paper's support for the interloper effect is Smurda and Haselton's 2002 talk at the Human Behavior and Evolution Society conference at Rutgers, which was never published and could not be obtained, together with Maner and colleagues' 2003 attention finding, which it calls additional suggestive evidence.

McKay and Efferson argue that the theory is vague about what a bias is, that it is unclear whether the cognitive biases it defends are anything more than behavioural biases, and that on that reading it reduces to expected utility theory. Their own proposal is that departures from Bayesian belief can be adaptive when they produce error-avoiding behaviour. Al-Shawaf, writing from inside the framework, shows that the sex-specific framing does not follow from it: what drives a bias is the cost matrix, so a father assessing his daughter's suitor should show commitment scepticism and a mother assessing her son's prospects should show sexual overperception. He calls these the sceptical dad and encouraging mom hypotheses and notes that they are untested. If a cost matrix can be assigned after the data arrive, the framework will fit any result.
misreadings:
The commonest error is to treat error management theory as a single effect with a single replication record. It is a way of generating hypotheses. Men's overperception of women's sexual intent was an established finding before the theory arrived, and the theory's own novel prediction was women's commitment scepticism, which has been tested far less.

The second is to cite Study 1 as evidence that men specifically overperceive women. It found no interaction between sex of rater and sex of target on the sexual-intent items. Men rated men as more sexually interested as well, and the paper says so. Only Study 2, with self-report as a second criterion, isolates the cross-sex effect.

The third is the sister correction. Men did rate their sisters far below other women, which is what was predicted. Women rated their brothers far below other men on a comparison for which no prediction had been made, and by a larger margin. A result that appears equally in the condition with no hypothesis attached is weak support for the hypothesis.

The fourth is to read the survey replications as evidence about perception. Bendixen and Hiraishi asked people how often the opposite sex had misjudged them. Women say it happens often and men say it rarely happens in that direction. Whether men's judgements are wrong is a separate question, and the studies that ask it, by comparing a rating against the target's own report, are where the sex difference thins out.

The fifth is to assume a bias in behaviour requires a bias in belief. Perilloux and Kurzban's position is that men may perceive accurately and act on low-probability chances anyway, which is error management working through action. Brandner and colleagues make the measurement version of the same point: difference scores cannot separate sensitivity from criterion, and when signal detection theory separated them on clear signals, sensitivity did the work.

The sixth is to count the framework's coverage as evidence for it. Haselton and Nettle review twelve domains and name only four effects that error management logic predicted in advance. Coverage after the fact is not the same as prediction, and the review does not say which of the other cases the theory came to first. A cost matrix chosen once the result is known can accommodate almost anything, which is Al-Shawaf's objection from inside the programme and McKay and Efferson's from outside.

The entry on agent detection rests on the same asymmetric-cost argument, that a false alarm is cheaper than a missed predator, and its record is worth comparing. There the framing prediction failed directly, since threat did not raise agent detection and the measured criterion was conservative. Here the target phenomenon is real and the argument about what causes it is unsettled. The seventh is to read that comparison as a verdict on the whole framework. The four failures collected here are all cases where the prediction was about perception or attention: agent detection, auditory looming, attention to disease cues and visual search for snakes. The one direct replication that succeeded, Moser and colleagues on weapon possession in 2025, asked instead how people rate another person's anger. The framework's record sorts by what kind of judgement is being predicted.
